grand_strategy.reading:
Jordan runs the grand strategy of a small, resource-poor monarchy whose
neighbours are bigger than its means and whose population is not the one its
state was built for. It has no leverage of its own, so it sells position: a
border no one else can hold, airspace over which wars are fought, a port, a
training ground, a seat for mediation, and a King who is received everywhere.
Everything is organised around one fear, that the Palestinian question be
settled on its territory - by annexation of the West Bank, by displacement
from Gaza, or by a security 'substitute' arrangement that makes the army the
jailer of the West Bank. That fear explains why a treaty partner of 32 years
is now treated as the main threat (no ambassadors since November 2023, the
energy-for-water swap refused, the annexation 'red line'), why the kingdom
still shoots down Iranian missiles over its own land, and why it will not
break with Tehran. The Luttwak pattern is that each safeguard enlarges the
exposure it was meant to cover: patrons make it a target, the ban on the
Brotherhood removes a valve, the aid corridor invites closure, the diplomatic
snub removes the leverage over the supplies that Israel can still cut. Two
signals that are not rows: the King travelled to Malaysia and Australia on
11 October 2026 while a Houthi strike on Riyadh airport killed a Jordanian,
so the King's presence abroad rather than at home is itself a choice; and
Israeli elections are due in October 2026, so the annexation threat will be
tested by the next coalition, not by this one.

After the Jordanian strikes on Daraa and Suwayda of 26 October 2026 the
Syrian border becomes the test of the Syria stance. Amman says it struck in
coordination with Damascus; Damascus says it did not, and closed the Nasib
crossing to passengers and trade. The strikes show the doctrine in its
plainest form (act across the line rather than wait for the other side to
hold it), and the closure is the price: the trade corridor of objective 6 is
the first casualty. No reopening was found by 29 October 2026, and no
statement by the foreign minister after the strikes was found.

stances.note: Treaty partner since the 1994 peace treaty (CRS: 'at peace since 1994'), but the relationship is at its lowest since before the treaty: no ambassadors on either side since November 2023 (Jordan refuses the return of Israel's and will not send its own), the water-for-energy swap refused in 2023, annexation of the West Bank called the King's 'red line', Jordanian planners reportedly weighing abrogation, and the Foreign Policy reading that Amman sees a bigger threat in Israel than in Iran. Not `rival` because the treaty, gas supply, the bridges, Gaza-aid coordination and the shared air screen against Iran still operate, and Amman aims its criticism at the current Israeli government, not the state; not `adversary` because nothing seeks Israel's destruction. `reluctant_partner` is the grade that records cooperation out of necessity while resisting alignment. Sources conflict on the energy deals: Foreign Policy says 'energy and water deals were canceled' (the 2021 swap is), while Jordan News (Oct 2026) still describes coordination on gas. Bond - grievance: the Palestinian question and the fear of an 'alternative homeland'. Israel's own grade of Jordan is not yet written.

stances.note: A warming partnership with the post-Assad government, built on border security rather than trust: foreign minister Safadi met al-Sharaa on 23 Dec 2024 ('stand by our Syrian brothers'), a joint security committee on border threats and drug smuggling was set up in January 2025, the King met al-Sharaa on 26 Feb 2025, Jordan hosted the Suwayda trilateral with Syria and the US (19 Jul, 12 Aug and 16 Sep 2025), and the water-sharing agreement of July 2025. Jordan struck smuggling sites in southern Syria on 24 Dec 2025 'in coordination with regional partners', and the second session of the Jordan-Syria Higher Coordination Council in Amman on 12 Apr 2026 signed 10 MoUs and a cooperation agreement and agreed a joint roadmap for Suwayda and the south (mirrored from the SYR card, whose reading of Jordan is partner / warming / bond none; a third session is set for Damascus in October 2026). Jordan is also a corridor for Qatari gas and Arab Gas Pipeline supplies. CRS adds that Amman publicly criticises Israeli incursions in Syria but privately assures Israel it will block Iran-backed groups, and that an electricity and gas deal could be revived after the repeal of the Caesar Act. Refugees: about 460,000 registered in Nov 2025, 173,000 returned in a year, about 345,000 in Oct 2026. Bond - affinity: Arab neighbour, tribal and trade ties. Update 29 Oct 2026 (trend moves from warming to cooling; grade unchanged): on 26 Oct Jordan's military struck what it called militant hideouts in Daraa and Suwayda and claimed more than 20 Islamic State militants killed (Reuters, 27 Oct). Syria said seven people died, three of them children and a woman, that the strikes were made without prior coordination and violated its sovereignty, and it closed the Nasib crossing to passengers and trade (Reuters, 27 Oct; Anadolu, 26 Oct). Amman says it acted in coordination with Damascus; Damascus denies it. The trend turns because the channel that carried the warming (border committees, the Higher Coordination Council) is now publicly disputed and the main crossing is shut. The grade stays partner because Damascus itself still announces a joint border security committee (Reuters, 27 Oct) and no source read describes rejection or reluctance. No reopening of the crossing was found in sources read up to 29 Oct 2026; no statement by the Jordanian foreign minister after the strikes was found (gap).

The Karak church attack was claimed by no group; Reuters reports only that authorities linked it to militants operating across the border, so the Islamic State link is Jordan's claim, not established. Syria denies the strikes were coordinated (its row toward JOR on the SYR file).
